tier_reason: randomgen's performance page (an independent third-party suite by the NumPy random maintainer, not the dSFMT authors) lists DSFMT Uniform 2.5 ns against MT19937 4.0 ns on a stated Cascade Lake 3.1 GHz CPU, and its generator script doc/source/performance.py is public (SIZE=25000, NUMBER=100, REPEAT=10, min taken). Compiler, compiler version and flags are not stated anywhere on the page or in the script, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Uniform doubles: DSFMT 2.5 ns per value against MT19937 4.0 ns per value, about 1.6x faster (derived from page data); against NumPy's legacy RandomState (5.2 ns) about 2.1x (derived from page data). Other rows of the same table: Uint32 2.8 vs 2.5 ns (slower), Uint64 4.2 vs 4.2 ns (equal), Expon 6.3 vs 6.1 ns (slower), Normal 10.1 vs 10.5 ns (about 1.04x faster, within noise; derived from page data), Gamma 25.1 vs 20.8 ns (slower). The SFMT row also shows Uniform 2.5 ns, so no gain over SFMT on this table.
corrections.workload: randomgen's doc/source/performance.py: Generator.random(size=25000) producing uniform doubles in [0,1) from the DSFMT and MT19937 bit generators, timeit.repeat with number=100 and repeat=10, minimum taken, reported as ns per value, driven through randomgen's Cython wrappers and NumPy's Generator around vendored copies of the C code.
corrections.caveats: Third-party numbers come from randomgen's Cython wrapper through NumPy's Generator (benchmark script doc/source/performance.py in bashtage/randomgen), so the win is for bulk uniform doubles only and includes Python call overhead; it measures randomgen's vendored copy of dSFMT, not a build of this repository. Compiler, compiler version and flags are not stated, which caps the tier at B. The MT19937 baseline is NumPy's implementation, not std::mt19937 or a fresh build of mt19937ar. randomgen's own page recommends against all Mersenne Twister variants (MT19937, MT64, SFMT, DSFMT) and shows SFC64, Xoshiro256 and PCG64DXSM faster still. The authors' own speed table and paper (Saito and Matsumoto, MCQMC 2008, claims dSFMT is fastest against MT, SFMT and WELL on 10^8 doubles) sit on math.sci.hiroshima-u.ac.jp, which was unreachable, so that claim is known only from a search snippet and is not recorded as evidence. The dSFMT repo README, CHANGE-LOG and html/index.html contain no timing numbers; test.c only times dSFMT against itself (clock() around fill_array calls). The 313.5% vs 72.5% 'speed-up relative to NumPy' rows in the archived randomstate README give a similar picture but no hardware.

notes: Numbers verified on randomgen's performance.rst (DSFMT and MT19937 rows) and the methodology on its doc/source/performance.py; only the Normal row needed a small correction (DSFMT is marginally faster there, not slower). Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE.txt, Hiroshima University), 43 stars, not a fork, last commit 2025-05-19 (merge of PR #7), so stale is right. Not a duplicate; related listed entries are mersennetwister-lab/sfmt (B) and bashtage/randomgen (C).

tier_reason: The 10x-500x (typical 40x) speedup and >5x memory savings over the original Cassowary solver appear only as first-party README and docs prose with no workload, hardware, compiler, Cassowary version or benchmark code against Cassowary; the repo's benchmarks/ (enaml_like_benchmark.cpp, g++ -std=c++11 -O2) time kiwi alone. One WebSearch found no independent head-to-head measurement.

corrections.caveats: Numbers only in README prose and mirrored in docs/source/index.rst and downstream package descriptions: no workload, hardware, compiler, flags, Cassowary version or benchmark code against Cassowary is published. The claim text is unchanged since at least kiwisolver 0.1.3 on PyPI (uploaded 2014-07-12), so the measurement dates from 2014 or earlier and was taken against the Cassowary code of that time. The repo's benchmarks directory (enaml_like_benchmark.cpp built by build_and_run_bench.sh with g++ -std=c++11 -O2, and a Python variant using perf) measures only kiwi itself, mainly to compare internal map types; they cannot reproduce the Cassowary comparison. The 2x speedup over std::map for kiwi's internal AssocVector-style sorted map is a sentence in docs/source/basis/solver_internals.rst with no table. amoeba (starwing, C) says it improves on kiwi's suggest path but gives no numbers. A JavaScript port line (kiwi.js and its fork lume/kiwi, listed in wave 13) is a separate entry, not a duplicate of this C++ project.
